title: Gross Negligence Penalty (GNP) - Canadian SR&ED Glossary
description: Read our Canadian SR&ED glossary to understand when the CRA assesses a Gross Negligence Penalty (GNP) on improper R&D tax claims.
summary: Canada's gross negligence penalty (GNP) under subsection 163(2) of the Income Tax Act applies to anyone who knowingly, or through gross negligence, makes a false statement or omission in an SR&ED claim. The CRA bears the burden of proof, and the penalty equals the greater of $100 or 50% of understated Part I tax and overstated refundable ITCs.

body.text: Canada's gross negligence penalty (GNP) under subsection 163(2) of the Income Tax Act applies to anyone who knowingly, or through gross negligence, makes a false statement or omission in an SR&ED claim. The CRA bears the burden of proof, and the penalty equals the greater of $100 or 50% of understated Part I tax and overstated refundable ITCs.

Between December 2024 and November 2026, Canada enacted the most consequential overhaul of its Scientific Research and Experimental Development (SR&ED) tax incentive programme in more than a decade. Following initial reform proposals in the December 16, 2024 Fall Economic Statement (FES 2024) and draft legislation released on August 15, 2025, the federal government tabled Budget 2025 on November 4, 2025, and enacted Bill C-15 (Budget Implementation Act, 2025, No. 1, S.C. 2026, c. 3), which received Royal Assent on March 26, 2026. Retroactive to taxation years beginning after December 15, 2024, Bill C-15 doubled the annual expenditure limit for the enhanced 35% refundable Investment Tax Credit (ITC) from $3,000,000 to $6,000,000 (superseding the $4,500,000 interim proposal in FES 2024), broadened the prior-year taxable capital phase-out thresholds from $10,000,000–$50,000,000 to $15,000,000–$75,000,000, extended the enhanced 35% refundable ITC to Eligible Canadian Public Corporations (ECPCs) using a three-year average gross revenue phase-out test, and restored the eligibility of capital expenditures and equipment lease costs incurred after December 15, 2024. Furthermore, on April 1, 2026, the CRA launched an optional Pre-Claim Approval Process offering upfront technical eligibility determinations within eight weeks. Most recently, Federal Budget 2026 (tabled in November 2026) proposed a further $930 million, five-year expansion of the SR&ED programme to cover regulatory pre-commercialization testing and intellectual property (IP) registration and maintenance expenses, complementing Québec's landmark consolidation of its provincial R&D incentives into the refundable Tax Credit for Research, Innovation and Commercialization (CRIC) for taxation years beginning after March 25, 2025.
1. Legislative Architecture and the 2024–2026 Statutory Reforms
1.1 Statutory Foundation under the Income Tax Act and Income Tax Regulations

Canada's federal R&D tax regime—the Scientific Research and Experimental Development (SR&ED) Tax Incentive Program—is codified within the federal Income Tax Act (R.S.C., 1985, c. 1 (5th Supp.), hereinafter the "ITA" or the "Act") and Part XXIX of the Income Tax Regulations (hereinafter the "ITR" or the "Regulations"). Unlike discretionary grant programmes, the SR&ED regime is an entitlement-based statutory tax incentive structured around two distinct, interlocking mechanisms: the Section 37 Pool of Deductible SR&ED Expenditures and the Section 127 / Section 127.1 Investment Tax Credit.

The first statutory pillar is the Pool of Deductible SR&ED Expenditures governed by Section 37 of the ITA. Subsection 37(1) permits a taxpayer carrying on a business in Canada in a taxation year to deduct current expenditures and—for property acquired after December 15, 2024—capital SR&ED expenditures incurred in Canada that are related to a business of the taxpayer. Expenditures accumulated in the Section 37 pool may be deducted in full or in part in the current taxation year to reduce net business income for tax purposes, or carried forward indefinitely to be deducted against business income in any subsequent taxation year, subject to loss restriction event rules under subsection 37(6.1) and mandatory current-year deduction rules for partnerships under paragraph 96(1)(e.1).

The second statutory pillar is the SR&ED Investment Tax Credit (ITC) governed by Sections 127 and 127.1 of the ITA. Section 127 enables taxpayers to earn an ITC calculated as a percentage (15% basic rate or 35% enhanced rate) of their "SR&ED qualified expenditure pool" at the end of the taxation year, as defined in subsection 127(9). Under subsection 127(5), non-refundable ITCs are deducted directly against federal Part I tax otherwise payable, with unused credits eligible for a 3-year carryback and a 20-year carryforward. Under Section 127.1 (specifically subsections 127.1(1), 127.1(2), and 127.1(2.01)), qualifying corporations, Canadian-controlled private corporations (CCPCs), Eligible Canadian Public Corporations (ECPCs), individuals, and certain trusts may receive all or a portion (100% or 40%) of their unapplied current-year ITCs as a direct cash refund.

The foundational technical definition of eligible R&D work is housed in subsection 248(1) of the ITA under the defined term "scientific research and experimental development". The rules governing the computation of allowable expenditures, the election between the Traditional Method and the Proxy Method, the calculation of the Prescribed Proxy Amount (PPA), the definition of Prescribed Depreciable Property (PDP), the exclusion of prescribed expenditures from ITC eligibility, and the designation of prescribed special-purpose buildings are codified in Sections 2900, 2902, and 2903 of the Income Tax Regulations.

body.text: 1.2 Chronology and Reconciliation of the 2024–2026 Legislative Reforms

Tax practitioners and corporate auditors reviewing historical and current documentation must carefully distinguish between three sequential policy milestones between December 2024 and November 2026, as several interim proposals were expanded prior to final legislative enactment.

First, on December 16, 2024, the federal government tabled the 2024 Fall Economic Statement (FES 2024), followed by detailed draft legislative proposals released by the Department of Finance on August 15, 2025, to revitalize the SR&ED programme for taxation years beginning on or after December 16, 2024 (that is, after December 15, 2024). FES 2024 and the August 2025 draft legislative notes initially proposed increasing the annual expenditure limit for the 35% enhanced ITC from $3,000,000 to $4,500,000 (which would have yielded a maximum annual refundable credit of $1,575,000), raising the prior-year taxable capital phase-out range from $10,000,000–$50,000,000 to $15,000,000–$75,000,000, extending the 35% enhanced refundable credit to Eligible Canadian Public Corporations (ECPCs) using a three-year average gross revenue phase-out ($15,000,000 to $75,000,000), and restoring the pre-2014 eligibility rules for capital expenditures and equipment lease costs incurred after December 15, 2024.

Second, on November 4, 2025, Minister of Finance and National Revenue François-Philippe Champagne presented Federal Budget 2025. Budget 2025 confirmed all of the structural expansions from FES 2024, with one major enhancement: instead of increasing the annual expenditure limit to $4,500,000, Budget 2025 doubled the expenditure limit from $3,000,000 to $6,000,000, raising the maximum annual refundable 35% ITC ceiling to $2,100,000. These amendments were enacted in Bill C-15 (An Act to implement certain provisions of the budget tabled in Parliament on November 4, 2025, Short Title: Budget Implementation Act, 2025, No. 1, S.C. 2026, c. 3), which received Royal Assent on March 26, 2026. All core rate, threshold, ECPC, and capital and lease restoration provisions took effect retroactively for taxation years beginning after December 15, 2024 (and for property acquired or lease amounts first becoming payable after December 15, 2024). Following Royal Assent, the CRA launched the optional Pre-Claim Approval Process on April 1, 2026, and issued revised versions of Form T661, Schedule T2SCH31, Schedule T2SCH49, Form T1145, Form T1146, and its core SR&ED policy manuals between May and October 2026.

Third, in November 2026, Federal Budget 2026 announced a $930 million, five-year expansion of the SR&ED programme specifically targeting the commercialization of Canadian innovation and domestic intellectual property retention, effective for taxation years beginning on or after Budget Day 2026. Specifically, Budget 2026 proposes to expand the scope of eligible SR&ED activities to include tests, technological validations, and studies conducted to meet regulatory requirements for obtaining an initial approval or certification necessary to commercialize a product or process, where directly related to an eligible SR&ED project. Furthermore, Budget 2026 proposes to introduce SR&ED eligibility for intellectual property (IP) protection expenditures—covering reasonable costs incurred in Canada (plus foreign IP office administrative fees) to prepare, file, register, and pay periodic maintenance fees for patents, certificates of supplementary protection, plant breeders' rights, or copyrighted software developed in the course of an eligible SR&ED project, while excluding IP litigation or enforcement costs and applying recapture rules if the IP is subsequently disposed of. Alongside the proposed SR&ED expansion, Budget 2026 confirmed the Productivity Mega Deduction announced on September 15, 2026 (expanding immediate expensing to cut the marginal effective tax rate on new business investment from 13% to 6.4%), and proposed the Canada Growth Incentive (providing a capital gains exemption of up to $15,000,000 per business per person on qualifying shares alongside enhanced section 44.1 small business share rollovers).
2. Statutory Definition of SR&ED and Technical Eligibility Framework
2.1 Analysis of Subsection 248(1) of the Income Tax Act

To qualify for federal SR&ED tax incentives, claimed activities must satisfy the statutory definition of "scientific research and experimental development" set out in subsection 248(1) of the Income Tax Act. The preamble to the definition establishes that SR&ED means "systematic investigation or search that is carried out in a field of science or technology by means of experiment or analysis". The definition is structured into four inclusive paragraphs—paragraphs (a), (b), (c), and (d)—followed by seven explicit statutory exclusions in paragraphs (e) through (k).

Under paragraph 248(1)(a), Basic Research encompasses work undertaken for the advancement of scientific knowledge without a specific practical application in view, typically conducted in laboratory or academic settings to uncover fundamental scientific principles, phenomena, or relationships without targeting a commercial product. Under paragraph 248(1)(b), Applied Research encompasses work undertaken for the advancement of scientific knowledge with a specific practical application in view, seeking to generate new scientific knowledge directed toward a commercial, medical, or industrial objective. Under paragraph 248(1)(c), Experimental Development—which accounts for the vast majority of corporate SR&ED claims—is defined as work undertaken for the purpose of achieving technological advancement for the purpose of creating new, or improving existing, materials, devices, products, or processes, explicitly including incremental improvements thereto.

Under paragraph 248(1)(d), Support Work encompasses work undertaken by or on behalf of the taxpayer with respect to eight exhaustive statutory categories—engineering, design, operations research, mathematical analysis, computer programming, data collection, testing, or psychological research—where the work is commensurate with the needs, and directly in support, of basic research, applied research, or experimental development described in paragraph (a), (b), or (c) that is undertaken in Canada by or on behalf of the taxpayer. Support work cannot qualify as SR&ED on a stand-alone basis; it is eligible only to the extent that it directly supports and is proportional to core paragraph (a), (b), or (c) SR&ED carried out in Canada.
2.2 Statutory Exclusions: Paragraphs 248(1)(e) to (k)

Even where a broad corporate undertaking involves technological innovation, seven categories of work are statutorily excluded from the definition of SR&ED under paragraphs 248(1)(e) through (k) and cannot be claimed. These exclusions are: (e) market research or sales promotion; (f) quality control or routine testing of materials, devices, products, or processes; (g) research in the social sciences or the humanities; (h) prospecting, exploring, or drilling for, or producing, minerals, petroleum, or natural gas; (i) the commercial production of a new or improved material, device, or product, or the commercial use of a new or improved process; (j) style changes; and (k) routine data collection.

In CRA technical audits, a recurring point of contention involves distinguishing between eligible support work under paragraph (d) (specifically testing and data collection) and excluded work under paragraphs (f) (quality control or routine testing) and (k) (routine data collection). Under the CRA Guidelines on the eligibility of work for scientific research and experimental development (SR&ED) tax incentives, the determinative legal criterion is purpose. Exclusions are evaluated only after establishing that core SR&ED work exists. If data collection or testing is carried out specifically to test a hypothesis or resolve a scientific or technological uncertainty within an active SR&ED project, it qualifies as eligible support work under paragraph (d). Conversely, if testing or data collection is conducted for commercial quality assurance, routine calibration, or normal business operations, it is excluded under paragraphs (f) or (k), subject to the proposed Budget 2026 expansion for regulatory commercialization testing and studies for taxation years beginning on or after Budget Day 2026.
2.3 CRA Administrative Framework: The "Why" and "How" Requirements

In its administrative guidance—Guidelines on the eligibility of work for scientific research and experimental development (SR&ED) tax incentives (which replaced the archived April 24, 2015 Eligibility of Work for SR&ED Investment Tax Credits Policy)—the CRA evaluates technical eligibility through two mandatory, sequential pillars: The "Why" Requirement and The "How" Requirement. Both requirements must be satisfied for work to qualify as SR&ED.
1. The "Why" Requirement (Scientific or Technological Advancement and Uncertainty)

The "Why" requirement examines the underlying purpose of the work, mandating that it be conducted for the advancement of scientific knowledge or for the purpose of achieving a technological advancement. The focus must be on generating or discovering conceptual knowledge (such as theories, causal relationships, or prediction models) rather than merely collecting factual knowledge (such as routine measurements). New scientific or technological knowledge is required only when a scientific or technological uncertainty exists—meaning that whether a given result or objective can be achieved, or how to achieve it, cannot be known or determined on the basis of available scientific or technological knowledge (combining internal company knowledge and publicly available knowledge).

In experimental development, common indicators of insufficient baseline knowledge include situations where existing design methods are inapplicable, requirements or specifications conflict with existing standards, too many variables or unknowns interact, operating parameters fall outside normal ranges, the problem evolves dynamically, data is not readily available, or interlocking constraints (including attempting to achieve functional objectives under strict economic or cost constraints) prevent standard solutions from working. Conversely, circumventing an uncertainty with a workaround using existing knowledge, or acquiring existing knowledge via training, hiring consultants or experts, on-the-job learning, or purchasing proprietary technology, does not qualify as attempting to achieve a technological advancement. Crucially, success or failure in achieving the desired objective is irrelevant; failed experiments that refute a hypothesis still advance technological knowledge and satisfy the "Why" requirement.
2. The "How" Requirement (Systematic Investigation or Search)

The "How" requirement governs the methodology employed to resolve the uncertainty: the work must be a systematic investigation or search carried out in a field of science or technology by means of experiment or analysis. Merely following standard design procedures or project protocols is not sufficient. Instead, a systematic investigation requires four sequential steps:

items: Generating an Idea or Hypothesis: Formulating a proposed method, approach, or solution consistent with known facts to serve as a starting point for further investigation toward resolving the uncertainty.
Testing by Experiment or Analysis: Testing the idea or hypothesis by means of structured experiment or analysis, allowing the hypothesis to evolve and change based on test findings.
Developing Logical Conclusions: Analysing the results or findings of the experiment or analysis to formulate logical scientific or technological conclusions.
Keeping Contemporaneous Evidence: Maintaining records and evidence that are generated as the work progresses.

body.text: 2.4 Project Boundaries, Shop Floor SR&ED, and the Budget 2026 Commercialization Expansion

When preparing Form T661, claimants must group eligible activities into discrete SR&ED Projects. The CRA distinguishes between a Company Project (a broader business undertaking with a commercial objective, such as expanding facilities or launching a product line) and an SR&ED Project, which exists as a subset comprising the interrelated activities necessary to attempt to achieve a specific scientific or technological advancement by overcoming scientific or technological uncertainty through systematic investigation. An SR&ED project begins when scientific or technological uncertainties are identified and specific objectives are established (which may include a technical feasibility study if followed up by experimentation or analysis) and ends when the uncertainty is resolved or determined to be unresolvable. Post-development troubleshooting, debugging, fine-tuning without technological uncertainty, customer facility installation, and end-user beta testing to confirm commercial specifications do not qualify. Where experimental development takes place in a manufacturing environment—referred to as "Shop Floor SR&ED"—claimants must segregate experimental trials from concurrent commercial production runs in accordance with the SR&ED During Production Runs Policy and the SR&ED while Developing an Asset Policy.

For taxation years beginning on or after Budget Day 2026, Federal Budget 2026 proposes to expand the downstream boundary of SR&ED projects in two targeted ways to support commercialization. First, eligible SR&ED activities would be expanded to include tests, technological validations, and studies conducted to meet regulatory requirements for obtaining an initial approval or certification necessary to commercialize a product or process, provided these activities relate directly to an eligible SR&ED project; standard SR&ED expenditure categories (wages, materials, contracts, overhead, and machinery and equipment) would apply to these activities. Second, eligible SR&ED expenditures would be expanded to include reasonable costs incurred to prepare, file, register, and pay periodic maintenance costs for intellectual property (IP) protection—specifically patents, certificates of supplementary protection, plant breeders' rights, or copyrighted software under Canadian or equivalent foreign legislation—for IP developed in the course of an eligible SR&ED project. Administrative fees paid to foreign IP offices would be eligible, but supporting activities (such as preparing an application) would have to be conducted within Canada, and IP enforcement or litigation costs would be excluded; if the taxpayer later disposes of the IP, recapture rules would apply to the related SR&ED deduction and ITC amounts.
3. Federal Investment Tax Credit Rates, Thresholds, Refundability, and Carryover Rules
3.1 Federal ITC Rate Structure: Enhanced (35%) vs. Basic (15%)

Under Section 127 of the ITA and the CRA SR&ED Investment Tax Credit Policy (updated October 7, 2026), federal SR&ED ITCs are computed at two statutory rates applied to a claimant's year-end SR&ED qualified expenditure pool minus any provincial super-allowance benefit amounts.

The Basic ITC Rate of 15%, governed by the definition of "investment tax credit" in subsection 127(9), applies generally to corporations that do not qualify for the enhanced rate (such as foreign-controlled corporations and large corporations exceeding the phase-out ceilings), to qualified expenditures of CCPCs and ECPCs that exceed their annual expenditure limit, and to unincorporated claimants including individuals (sole proprietorships), partnerships (allocated to eligible partners under subsection 127(8)), and trusts.

The Enhanced ITC Rate of 35%, governed by subsection 127(10.1), provides an additional 20% ITC on top of the 15% basic rate on qualified SR&ED expenditures up to the corporation's annual Expenditure Limit. For taxation years beginning before December 16, 2024, only Canadian-controlled private corporations (CCPCs) could earn the 35% enhanced rate. Effective for taxation years beginning after December 15, 2024 (enacted under Bill C-15, S.C. 2026, c. 3), subsection 127(10.1) was amended to extend the 35% enhanced rate to Eligible Canadian Public Corporations (ECPCs) as well.
3.2 Expenditure Limit Mechanics and Phase-Out Formulas ($6,000,000 Ceiling)

Under Bill C-15 (S.C. 2026, c. 3, Royal Assent March 26, 2026), the maximum annual Expenditure Limit on which a qualifying CCPC or ECPC (and its associated corporate group) can earn the enhanced 35% ITC was doubled from $3,000,000 to $6,000,000 for taxation years beginning after December 15, 2024. Consequently, the maximum annual federal refundable ITC at the 35% rate doubled from $1,050,000 ($3,000,000 at 35%) to $2,100,000 ($6,000,000 at 35%). Associated CCPCs must allocate the $6,000,000 expenditure limit among group members using Schedule T2SCH49 (Agreement Among Associated Canadian-Controlled Private Corporations to Allocate the Expenditure Limit, updated May 29, 2026). Depending on corporate classification and taxpayer election, the $6,000,000 expenditure limit is subject to one of two statutory phase-out structures for taxation years beginning after December 15, 2024.
1. The Taxable Capital Phase-Out Structure for CCPCs (Subsection 127(10.2))

For CCPCs that do not elect into the gross revenue structure, the annual expenditure limit is phased out on a straight-line basis based on the taxable capital employed in Canada (on an associated group basis) for the immediately preceding taxation year. For taxation years beginning before December 16, 2024, the $3,000,000 expenditure limit began phasing out when prior-year taxable capital employed in Canada exceeded $10,000,000 and was completely eliminated at $50,000,000. Under Bill C-15, for taxation years beginning after December 15, 2024, the prior-year taxable capital phase-out thresholds were increased to $15,000,000 and $75,000,000 (a $60,000,000 phase-out band). While the interim $4,500,000 proposal in FES 2024 reduced the limit by $0.075 per $1.00 of taxable capital above $15,000,000, under the enacted $6,000,000 expenditure limit in Budget 2025 and Bill C-15, the limit is reduced on a straight-line basis across the $60,000,000 band ($0.10 per $1.00 of prior-year taxable capital employed in Canada between $15,000,000 and $75,000,000), reaching nil at $75,000,000:
CCPC Expenditure Limit = $6,000,000 × (($60,000,000 − max($0, min($60,000,000, Prior-Year Taxable Capital − $15,000,000))) ÷ $60,000,000)

Additionally, under subsection 127.1(2), the "qualifying income limit"—which determines whether a CCPC is a "qualifying corporation" eligible for 40% refundability on its 15% basic ITC earned above the expenditure limit—was updated for taxation years beginning after December 15, 2024, to reflect the $60,000,000 phase-out band above $15,000,000 (replacing the pre-December 16, 2024 denominator of $40,000,000 above $10,000,000):
where A is nil if prior-year taxable capital employed in Canada does not exceed $15,000,000, or the lesser of $60,000,000 and the amount by which prior-year taxable capital exceeds $15,000,000.
2. Eligible Canadian Public Corporations (ECPCs) and the Gross Revenue Phase-Out Structure (Subsection 127(10.6))

To ensure Canadian public companies can access refundable R&D support, Bill C-15 introduced the defined term "eligible Canadian public corporation" (ECPC) in subsection 127(9) and extended the 35% enhanced refundable ITC to ECPCs for taxation years beginning after December 15, 2024. To qualify as an ECPC throughout a taxation year, a corporation must: (1) be resident in Canada; (2) have a class of shares listed on a designated stock exchange (or have elected, or been designated by the Minister of National Revenue, to be a public corporation); and (3) not be controlled, directly or indirectly in any manner whatever, by one or more non-resident persons. Additionally, Canadian-resident corporations all or substantially all (90% or more) of whose shares are owned by one or more ECPCs are also eligible for the enhanced refundable ITC.

Under subsection 127(10.6), an ECPC's $6,000,000 expenditure limit is phased out on a straight-line basis when the corporation's (or consolidated corporate group's) average annual gross revenue over the three preceding fiscal years is between $15,000,000 and $75,000,000, reaching nil at $75,000,000:
ECPC / Gross Revenue Expenditure Limit = $6,000,000 × (($60,000,000 − max($0, min($60,000,000, 3-Year Average Gross Revenue − $15,000,000))) ÷ $60,000,000)

For corporate groups that prepare consolidated financial statements (defined in subsection 127(9) as financial statements in which the assets, liabilities, income, expenses, and cash flows of the members of a group are presented as those of a single economic entity), gross revenue is measured based on the amounts reported in the group financial statements at the highest level of consolidation, and group members must share the expenditure limit. Unconsolidated companies measure gross revenue using GAAP financial statements presented to shareholders, and where a corporation has fewer than three preceding fiscal years, average annual revenue is calculated over the actual number of preceding fiscal years (one or two fiscal years).

Crucially, under subsections 127(10.31) and 127(10.32), a CCPC has the option to formally elect to have its expenditure limit determined under the gross revenue phase-out structure rather than the taxable capital structure. Where a CCPC group makes this election for a taxation year, the taxable capital phase-out under subsection 127(10.2) does not apply, allowing capital-intensive CCPCs with high equity or debt capital but modest gross revenues to preserve access to the full $6,000,000 expenditure limit.
3.3 Comprehensive Federal ITC Refundability Matrix (Section 127.1)

The cash refundability of earned federal SR&ED ITCs is governed by Section 127.1 of the ITA—specifically the definitions of "qualifying corporation", "excluded corporation", and "refundable investment tax credit" in subsection 127.1(2) and the additional refundability provisions in subsection 127.1(2.01). Under the post-December 15, 2024 rules enacted by Bill C-15, while current expenditures (and the PPA) earning the 35% enhanced ITC attract a 100% refund rate, restored capital expenditures earning the 35% enhanced ITC attract a 40% refund rate. Furthermore, under subsection 127.1(2.01), both a Non-Qualifying CCPC (a CCPC that is neither a qualifying corporation nor an excluded corporation) and an ECPC receive 100% refundability on the 35% ITC earned on current expenditures and 40% refundability on the 35% ITC earned on capital expenditures up to their expenditure limit; however, only a Qualifying CCPC receives 40% refundability on the 15% basic ITC earned on expenditures exceeding the expenditure limit.

body.text: 3.4 Special Rules for Partnerships (Section 96 and Subsection 127(8))

Under paragraph 96(1)(a) and subsection 248(1) of the ITA and the CRA SR&ED Claims for Partnerships Policy, a partnership is not a separate legal entity or taxpayer and does not file an income tax return, but its net income or loss is computed as if the partnership were a separate person. Because the SR&ED work is legally considered to be performed by the partnership itself rather than its partners, the SR&ED ITC allocated from a partnership under subsection 127(8) and paragraph 127(9)(b) can only be earned at the basic 15% rate, even if the partner receiving the allocation is a CCPC or a qualifying corporation.

Furthermore, under paragraph 96(1)(e.1) and subsection 37(1), a partnership is not permitted to carry forward any balance in its pool of deductible SR&ED expenditures to a subsequent fiscal period; the entire Section 37 pool balance at the end of the partnership's fiscal period must be deducted in calculating the partnership's net income or loss for that year. Under subsection 127(12.1), the allocation of an SR&ED ITC from a partnership reduces the partnership's Section 37 pool in that same fiscal period, regardless of whether a partner claims the ITC against Part I tax or receives a refund. Any salary or wages paid to a partner are treated as a distribution of income and cannot be claimed as SR&ED salary or wages.

Under subsection 127(8) and the definition of "specified member" in subsection 248(1), no SR&ED ITC may be allocated to a specified member of the partnership—which includes any limited partner (defined in subsection 96(2.4)) and any general partner who was not regularly, continuously, and substantially actively engaged in the operating activities of the partnership's business (other than financing) during the tax year. Under subsection 96(2.4), a partnership loss created or increased by deducting the Section 37 SR&ED expenditure pool is denied to a limited partner. Additionally, because a partnership is not a taxpayer, it cannot transfer or receive qualified SR&ED expenditures under a non-arm's length contract under subsection 127(13).
3.5 Carryover Periods, Section 37 Pool Dynamics, and Loss Restriction Events
1. Carryback and Carryforward of Unused ITCs

Under subsection 127(5) and the definition of "investment tax credit" in subsection 127(9), any portion of an SR&ED ITC earned in a taxation year that exceeds the amount required to reduce current-year federal Part I tax to nil and is not refunded as a cash credit under Section 127.1 (since any refunded ITC is deemed by subsection 127.1(3) to have been applied to reduce Part I tax) may be carried back up to 3 preceding taxation years (reported in Part 12 of Schedule T2SCH31) or carried forward up to 20 subsequent taxation years to reduce Part I tax otherwise payable.
2. Mechanics of the Section 37 Deductible Pool

The cumulative pool of deductible SR&ED expenditures under subsection 37(1) (calculated in Part 3, Section C of Form T661) allows non-partnership claimants to deduct all, a portion, or none of the available pool balance in the current year and carry forward any remaining positive balance indefinitely. The pool is increased by current-year allowable current expenditures in Canada (paragraph 37(1)(a)), allowable capital expenditures in Canada acquired after December 15, 2024 (paragraph 37(1)(b)), repayments of government or non-government assistance that previously reduced the pool (paragraph 37(1)(c)), prior-year negative pool income inclusions under paragraph 12(1)(v) (paragraph 37(1)(c.1)), and prior-year recaptured ITC amounts added to tax payable under subsections 127(27), (29), or (34) (paragraph 37(1)(c.2)) or partnership recapture excesses under subsection 127(30) (paragraph 37(1)(c.3)).

Conversely, the Section 37 pool is decreased by government and non-government assistance received, receivable, or reasonably expected to be received at the filing-due date (paragraph 37(1)(d)), provincial super-allowance benefit amounts (paragraph 37(1)(d.1)), federal SR&ED ITCs applied against Part I tax and/or refunded in the preceding taxation year attributable to the PPA, qualified current expenditures, or transferred qualified expenditures (paragraph 37(1)(e) / Line 435 of Form T661), amounts deducted under subsection 37(1) in preceding taxation years (paragraph 37(1)(f)), insolvency deductions under section 61.3 (paragraph 37(1)(f.1)), and loss restriction event reductions (paragraph 37(1)(h)). If the Section 37 pool balance is negative at the end of a taxation year, paragraph 12(1)(v) mandates that the negative amount be included in computing business income for that year, resetting the opening pool balance for the subsequent taxation year to nil.
3. Loss Restriction Events / Acquisition of Control (Subsection 37(6.1))

If a corporation or trust undergoes a loss restriction event (such as an acquisition of control of a corporation or a change in majority-interest beneficiary of a trust), paragraph 37(1)(h) and subsection 37(6.1) restrict the taxpayer's ability to carry forward and deduct unused pre-acquisition Section 37 pool balances, limiting future deductions to income derived from that same business (or similar businesses) carried on for profit or with a reasonable expectation of profit.
4. Qualifying Expenditures (QREs), Overhead Methodologies, and Capital Restoration
4.1 Overhead Election: The Traditional Method vs. The Proxy Method

Under subsection 37(8) and subsection 37(10) of the ITA and Section 2900 of the ITR, a claimant must select one of two methods on Lines 160 and 162 of Form T661 to compute SR&ED expenditures for each taxation year. The election between the Traditional Method and the Proxy Method is made on a year-by-year basis; claimants are not locked into the method chosen in prior years, but once Form T661 is filed for a specific taxation year, the choice for that year is irrevocable. If the Proxy Method is not explicitly elected on Line 160 when the initial claim for the year is filed, the Traditional Method applies automatically.

body.text: 4.2 Deep-Dive: The Proxy Method and Prescribed Proxy Amount (55% PPA)

Under subsection 2900(4) of the Income Tax Regulations and the CRA Prescribed Proxy Amount Policy, claimants electing the Proxy Method compute a notional overhead amount—the Prescribed Proxy Amount (PPA)—in Part 5 of Form T661. The PPA is equal to 55% of the claimant's SR&ED Salary Base (calculated on Line 818, multiplied by 55% on Line 820, and carried to Line 502 in Part 4):
Prescribed Proxy Amount (Line 820 / Line 502) = 55% × Salary Base (Line 818)

The Salary Base (Line 818) is the sum of Line 814—which includes qualifying salary or wages of employees (other than specified employees) directly engaged in SR&ED—and Line 816—which includes the allowable salary or wages of specified employees directly engaged in SR&ED, subject to the 75% maximum time cap and the 2.5 × YMPE ceiling (and excluding bonuses, remuneration based on profits, taxable benefits, and prior-year unpaid wages paid in the year).

Because the PPA is a notional amount that replaces actual overhead expenses (such as office supplies, heat, water, electricity, telephones, support staff wages, non-SR&ED trade contracts, employer share of benefits, travel, training, property taxes, and facility maintenance), neither the PPA nor the actual overhead expenditures it represents can be included in the Section 37 pool of deductible SR&ED expenditures; instead, actual overhead expenses are deducted as ordinary business expenses. However, the PPA is included in qualified SR&ED expenditures on Line 502 to earn the SR&ED ITC, and any ITC earned on the PPA and applied or refunded in a taxation year reduces the Section 37 pool in the following taxation year under subparagraph 37(1)(e)(i). Finally, the calculated PPA is subject to an overall cap to ensure that the sum of qualified SR&ED expenditures, the PPA, and other specified deductions does not exceed total business expenditures made in the taxation year.
4.3 Deep-Dive: The Traditional Method Overhead Rules (Regulation 2900(2)(c) and 2900(3)(b))

Under the Traditional Method, a claimant enters "0" on Line 502 and claims actual SR&ED overhead and other current expenditures on Line 360 of Form T661. Under subclause 37(8)(a)(ii)(A)(II) of the ITA, paragraph 2900(2)(c) and paragraph 2900(3)(b) of the ITR, and the CRA SR&ED Overhead and Other Expenditures Policy, an expenditure (or a rational, reasonable portion thereof) qualifies on Line 360 only if it satisfies two cumulative tests:

items: The "Directly Related" Test: The expenditure must be directly related to the prosecution of SR&ED in Canada, requiring a direct linkage—with no intervening step or intermediary—to the SR&ED work, the SR&ED staff, or the machinery and equipment used by staff to perform SR&ED.
The "Incremental" Test: The expenditure would not have been incurred had such prosecution of SR&ED not occurred.

body.text: Under these two tests, eligible Line 360 overhead items include the employer's share of related benefits directly linked to hands-on SR&ED employees (whereas benefits, travel, and training for clerical or administrative staff are disallowed as indirect); clerical and administrative salaries (such as HR, accounting, or purchasing) only where directly linked and incremental to ongoing SR&ED claimed in the year; non-SR&ED contract costs (such as electricians, welders, and mechanics) directly related and incremental to SR&ED (whereas fixed-cost maintenance contracts fail the incremental test); incremental utilities and identifiable incremental long-distance telephone or internet charges (whereas fixed monthly telephone/internet plans are excluded); training and travel in Canada for hands-on SR&ED staff; periodical subscriptions; fees paid to clinical study volunteers; health and safety expenses; moving/relocation expenses to relocate SR&ED employees to another facility; retiring allowances directly attributable to SR&ED employees; and active SR&ED waste disposal costs incurred during the project. Conversely, under Section 2902 of the ITR, prescribed expenditures—including fees for preparing SR&ED claims, costs to attend conventions or conferences, interest expenses, legal and accounting fees, entertainment, advertising, selling expenses, and fines or penalties—are strictly excluded from ITC calculations even if incremental.
4.4 Salaries and Wages, Specified Employees, YMPE Caps, and the 10% Foreign Rule

Under subsection 248(1) of the ITA and the CRA SR&ED Salary or Wages Policy (updated January 28, 2025), "salary or wages" means income of a taxpayer from an office or employment as computed under subdivision a of Division B of Part I of the Act. It includes regular wages, vacation pay, statutory holiday pay, sick leave pay, pay in lieu of termination notice, tips, honorariums, director's and management fees, commissions, cash outlays for taxable benefits under section 6 (excluding any GST/HST input tax credit or PST rebate under subsection 248(16)), inducements or non-competition payments, and—for employees other than specified employees—bonuses and remuneration based on profits. It excludes the employer's share of related benefits, extended vacation or sick leave, stock option benefits, and retiring allowances. If an employee spends all or substantially all (at least 90%) of their working time directly engaged in SR&ED in Canada, 100% of their eligible salary or wages qualifies.
1. Strict Statutory Limits for "Specified Employees"

A "specified employee" (an employee who is a specified shareholder owning 10% or more of the shares of any class of the corporation or a related corporation, or who does not deal at arm's length with the employer) is subject to strict statutory limitations on Form T661. First, when computing allowable SR&ED salary or wages on Line 305 (under both the Traditional and Proxy Methods), bonuses and remuneration based on profits are excluded, and the maximum allowable SR&ED salary per specified employee is capped under subsection 37(9.1) at 5 times the Year's Maximum Pensionable Earnings (YMPE) (under section 18 of the Canada Pension Plan) for the calendar year in which the taxation year ends, prorated by the number of days in the taxation year during which the individual was a specified employee:
Specified Employee Salary Cap (Subsection 37(9.1)) = A × (B ÷ 365)

where A is 5 times the YMPE for the calendar year and B is the number of days in the taxation year during which the individual was a specified employee. If an individual is a specified employee of two or more associated corporations, no amount may be claimed under subsection 37(9.2) unless the associated corporations file under subsection 37(9.3) Form T1174 (Agreement Between Associated Corporations to Allocate Salary or Wages of Specified Employees for Scientific Research and Experimental Development (SR&ED)) accompanied by a directors' resolution (or sole shareholder confirmation) allocating the 5 × YMPE cap.

Second, when computing the Salary Base (Line 816 / Line 818) for the 55% Prescribed Proxy Amount under the Proxy Method (Part 5, Table 7 of Form T661), the amount included for each specified employee is further restricted to the lesser of:

items: Column 4 (75% Time Cap): The specified employee's eligible salary or wages (excluding bonuses, remuneration based on profits, taxable benefits, and prior-year unpaid wages paid in the year) multiplied by the percentage of time spent directly engaged in SR&ED, capped at a maximum of 75%; OR
Column 5 (2.5 × YMPE Cap): A maximum allowable limit equal to 2.5 times the YMPE prorated by the number of days employed in the taxation year:

body.text: 2. Unpaid Remuneration (Subsection 78(4)) and Unpaid Amounts (Subsection 127(26))

Under subsection 78(4) of the ITA, employee remuneration that is not paid within 180 days from the end of the taxation year in which the expense was incurred is deemed not to have been incurred in that taxation year, and cannot be included in the pool of deductible SR&ED expenditures until the subsequent year in which it is actually paid. Similarly, under subsection 127(26) and the CRA Total Qualified SR&ED Expenditures for Investment Tax Credit Purposes Policy, current expenditures (other than salary or wages) incurred in a taxation year but not paid within 180 days of the taxation year-end are deducted when calculating qualified expenditures for ITC purposes; to be added to qualified expenditures in the subsequent year when paid (at 80% for arm's length contracts), the unpaid amount must have been identified on Form T661 within the 18-month reporting deadline for the original year incurred, or else it is permanently excluded from ITC calculations.
3. Permissible Foreign SR&ED Salaries (10% Rule – Subsections 37(1.4) and 37(1.5))

Under subsections 37(1.4) and 37(1.5) of the ITA and Section 10.0 of the SR&ED Salary or Wages Policy, permissible salary or wages for SR&ED work performed outside Canada are deemed to be made in Canada (reported on Line 307 for non-specified employees and Line 309 for specified employees) up to the lesser of Amount A and Amount B:

items: Amount A (Total Qualifying Foreign SR&ED Wages): Salary or wages for SR&ED carried on outside Canada where: (a) the work was directly undertaken by an employee of the claimant (not a contractor); (b) the employee was a resident of Canada when the expense was incurred; (c) the work was related to a business of the claimant; (d) the foreign work was an integral part of, and solely in support of, SR&ED carried on in Canada; and (e) the salary or wages were not subject to income or profits tax from another country.

Amount B (10% Limit): 10% of the total SR&ED salary or wages for SR&ED carried on in Canada (measured using Line 306 of Form T661, plus any direct undertaking, supervisory, or support salaries claimed as overhead on Line 360 under the Traditional Method, excluding clerical and administrative salaries).

body.text: 4.5 Materials Consumed vs. Materials Transformed (CRA Materials for SR&ED Policy)

Under subclauses 37(8)(a)(ii)(A)(I)/(II) and 37(8)(a)(ii)(B)(V) of the ITA, paragraph 2900(2)(a) of the ITR, and the CRA Materials for SR&ED Policy, the cost of materials consumed or transformed in the prosecution of SR&ED in Canada is 100% deductible in the Section 37 pool and 100% eligible for the SR&ED ITC under both the Traditional and Proxy Methods. To qualify as "materials for SR&ED", the items must be physical and tangible (in a solid, liquid, or gaseous state) and must at a given moment in the SR&ED process compose the body of a tangible object on which the SR&ED is being carried out or that results from the SR&ED. Broken or used lab supplies (petri dishes, beakers, flasks, pipettes), cleaning supplies, CDs/DVDs, used lubricants, utility water, boiler feed water, and energy (gas, electricity, propane) used to power equipment or heat a laboratory do not compose the body of a thing and are excluded from materials (though potentially claimable as Line 360 overhead under the Traditional Method), whereas process water (water entering a chemical equation to become part of a product), seed, growth media, agar, fungal cultures, animal feed, and field-plot fertilizers or pesticides qualify as materials.

Form T661 distinguishes between Materials Consumed (Line 320)—materials destroyed, used up, or rendered virtually valueless during SR&ED, which do not attract recapture—and Materials Transformed (Line 325)—materials incorporated into another product, custom asset, or prototype that has value to the claimant or another party, which are subject to ITC recapture under subsections 127(27) to (36) if sold or converted to commercial use. The claimable cost is the laid-down cost (invoice cost, customs and excise duties, transportation, storage, and pre-testing processing services such as metal galvanization, or raw materials, direct labour, and production overhead for internally manufactured inventory), and can only be claimed in the taxation year in which the materials are actually consumed or transformed in SR&ED (and paid within 180 days of year-end for ITC purposes).
4.6 Subcontractor Expenditures and Third-Party Payments (80% ITC Rule and Form T1146)
1. Arm's Length SR&ED Contracts (Line 340 – 80% ITC Inclusion)

Under subparagraph 37(1)(a)(i.01) and the CRA Contract Expenditures for SR&ED Performed on Behalf of a Claimant Policy, when a claimant contracts an arm's length party to perform SR&ED on its behalf in Canada (where the work is controlled by the payer and rights are exclusive to the payer), 100% of the SR&ED contract expenditure is deductible in the Section 37 pool (Line 340), and 80% qualifies to earn an SR&ED ITC (after the 20% reduction on Line 529 of Form T661), provided the contractor is a taxable supplier. A payer may claim arm's length contract expenditures for paragraph 248(1)(d) support work that is commensurate with the needs and directly in support of the payer's Canadian SR&ED, even though the contractor cannot claim stand-alone support work for itself. The arm's length contractor must reduce its own qualified SR&ED expenditures by the "contract payment" received or receivable under subsection 127(9).
2. Non-Arm's Length (NAL) SR&ED Contracts (Line 345 & Form T1146)

When a claimant enters into an SR&ED contract with a non-arm's length (NAL) performer (section 251), the claimant's expenditure is an allowable Section 37 expenditure (Line 345), but does not qualify for the claimant's ITC (deducted on Line 541). Instead, the NAL performer claims its own underlying SR&ED expenditures without reduction for the contract payment (and under subsection 37(13), support work performed by an NAL contractor is deemed to be SR&ED if it would be SR&ED when performed by the payer). However, under subsection 127(13), the NAL performer and payer may jointly file Form T1146 (Agreement to Transfer Qualified Expenditures Incurred in Respect of SR&ED Contracts Between Persons Not Dealing at Arm's Length, updated May 15, 2026) to transfer all or part of the performer's qualified expenditures (up to the contract amount) to the payer for ITC purposes (reported on Line 540 by the performer and Line 510 by the payer). Subsection 127(24) prevents circumventing NAL rules through an arm's length intermediary.
3. Third-Party Payments (Line 370 & Form T1263 – 80% ITC Inclusion)

Under subparagraphs 37(1)(a)(i.1), (ii), and (iii) and the CRA Third-Party Payments Policy, a "third-party payment" is a payment made for SR&ED in Canada not directly undertaken by or on behalf of the claimant (the performer controls the work and the claimant receives non-exclusive preferential rights to exploit the results), provided the SR&ED is related to a business of the claimant and the claimant is entitled to exploit the results. Eligible recipients comprise Entity A (a corporation resident in Canada, subparagraph 37(1)(a)(i.1)), Entity B (an approved association, clause 37(1)(a)(ii)(A)), Entity C (an approved university, college, research institute, or similar institution, clause 37(1)(a)(ii)(B)), Entity D (a non-profit SR&ED corporation exempt under paragraph 149(1)(j), clause 37(1)(a)(ii)(C) and subparagraph 37(1)(a)(iii)), and Entity E (an approved granting council/organization making payments to B, C, or D entities, clause 37(1)(a)(ii)(E)). Third-party payments are 100% deductible in the Section 37 pool (Line 370) and 80% eligible for the SR&ED ITC (after the 20% reduction on Line 529), and require filing Form T1263 for each payment rather than completing Part 2 of Form T661.
4.7 Restoration of Capital Expenditures, Shared-Use Equipment (SUE), Lease Costs, and Recapture (Post-December 15, 2024)

Enacted via Bill C-15 (S.C. 2026, c. 3), Parliament restored the eligibility of SR&ED capital expenditures, Shared-Use Equipment (SUE), and equipment lease costs for property acquired (and available for use) or lease amounts first becoming payable after December 15, 2024 (that is, on or after December 16, 2024), while repealing subsections 37(14) and 37(15) (the post-2013 capital look-through rules for contracts and third-party payments).
1. SR&ED Capital Expenditures: The "All or Substantially All" (ASA ≥90%) Intent Test

Under restored paragraph 37(1)(b), subclauses 37(8)(a)(ii)(A)(III) (Traditional Method) and 37(8)(a)(ii)(B)(III) (Proxy Method), Regulation 2902(b), and the CRA SR&ED Capital Expenditures Policy (updated June 29, 2026), an expenditure to acquire depreciable property after December 15, 2024, qualifies as an SR&ED capital expenditure (claimed on Line 390 of Form T661 for the Section 37 pool and Line 535 for qualified expenditures, with the 10 most expensive properties reported on Lines 262 and 263) if, at the time of acquisition, the claimant intended to either:

items: Use the property during all or substantially all (ASA, defined as 90% or more) of its operating time in its expected useful life in the prosecution of SR&ED in Canada; OR

Consume all or substantially all (90% or more) of its value in the prosecution of SR&ED in Canada (such as property used in developing a prototype or pilot plant that retains less than 10% life expectancy or value afterward).

body.text: Under subsection 37(1.2), capital property is not eligible until it becomes available for use, and under subsection 37(6), amounts deducted under subsection 37(1) for capital property are deemed to be Capital Cost Allowance (CCA) in a separate prescribed class (so the property cannot be claimed on Schedule T2SCH8). Crucially, used depreciable property (property previously used or acquired for use or lease for any purpose before acquisition by the claimant) qualifies for immediate deduction in the Section 37 pool on Line 390, but is a prescribed expenditure under Regulation 2902(b) that does not qualify for SR&ED ITCs on Line 535. Furthermore, land is excluded from paragraph 37(1)(b), and buildings or leasehold interests in buildings are excluded under paragraph 37(8)(e), except for a prescribed special-purpose building under Regulation 2903. For CCPCs and ECPCs earning the 35% enhanced rate, ITCs on new ASA capital property are 40% refundable.
2. Shared-Use Equipment (SUE) (Subsection 127(9) & CRA Policy Updated May 22, 2026)

Under subsection 127(9) of the ITA and the CRA SR&ED Shared-Use-Equipment Policy (updated May 22, 2026), brand-new depreciable machinery or equipment acquired after December 15, 2024, that does not meet the 90% ASA intent test (and is neither General Purpose Office Equipment or Furniture (GPOEF) nor Prescribed Depreciable Property (PDP) under Regulation 2900(11)) qualifies as Shared-Use Equipment (SUE) on Line 504 (and Part 6C Box 792 for the 20 most expensive SUE items) if it is actually used primarily—more than 50% but less than 90%—of its operating time for SR&ED in Canada across two statutory periods:

items: First-Term SUE: If used primarily (>50%) for SR&ED during the First Period—beginning when the property becomes available for use and ending at the end of the first taxation year ending at least 12 months after that time—then 1/4 (25%) of the capital cost qualifies for the SR&ED ITC in that taxation year.

Second-Term SUE: If the property qualified as First-Term SUE and is used primarily (>50%) for SR&ED during the Second Period—beginning when the property becomes available for use and ending at the end of the first taxation year ending at least 24 months after that time—an additional 1/4 (25%) of the capital cost (50% cumulative) qualifies for the SR&ED ITC in that second taxation year.

body.text: The capital cost of SUE is not included in the Section 37 pool; instead, it is depreciated under normal CCA rules on Schedule T2SCH8.
3. Equipment Lease Expenditures (Post-December 15, 2024 Rules)

Under the CRA SR&ED Lease Expenditures Policy (updated June 22, 2026), equipment lease costs incurred after December 15, 2024, qualify based on the overhead method elected. Under the Traditional Method, if leased equipment is used 90% or more (ASA) of its operating time for SR&ED in Canada, 100% of the lease cost is claimed as a lease expenditure (subclause 37(8)(a)(ii)(A)(I)); if used less than 90% of the time for SR&ED, the proportional operating-time percentage is claimed on Line 360 as overhead if directly related and incremental (subclause 37(8)(a)(ii)(A)(II)). Under the Proxy Method, if leased equipment (excluding GPOEF) is used 90% or more (ASA) of its operating time for SR&ED in Canada, 100% of the lease cost is claimed (subclause 37(8)(a)(ii)(B)(I)); if used primarily—more than 50% but less than 90%—of its operating time for SR&ED, 50% of the lease cost is claimed (subclause 37(8)(a)(ii)(B)(VI)); and if used 50% or less of the time, 0% can be claimed. Building rent is excluded under paragraph 37(8)(e) unless the building is a prescribed special-purpose building under Regulation 2903, whereas under Data Kinetics Ltd. v. The Queen, dedicated telecommunications bandwidth qualifies as a lease of equipment under the Proxy Method.
4. Recapture of SR&ED Investment Tax Credits (Subsections 127(27) to 127(36))

Under subsections 127(27) to 127(36) and the CRA Recapture of SR&ED Investment Tax Credit Policy, if a claimant disposes of or converts to commercial use a property on which an SR&ED ITC was earned within the 20 preceding taxation years—including materials transformed, ASA capital equipment, Shared-Use Equipment, property acquired under an SR&ED contract, or (under the Budget 2026 proposals) registered IP for which IP protection costs were claimed—the lesser of the ITC earned or the applicable ITC percentage of the proceeds of disposition (or fair market value) is recaptured by adding the amount directly to Part I tax payable for the year of disposition or conversion, while correspondingly increasing the Section 37 deductible pool in the following year under paragraph 37(1)(c.2). Salaries, wages, overhead, and materials consumed are never subject to recapture, and CRA policy waives recapture on experimental products sold for scrap or converted at a fair market value of less than 10% of cost.
5. Government Assistance, Non-Government Assistance, and Grant Stacking Mechanics
5.1 Statutory Framework for Assistance and Contract Payments (Paragraph 37(1)(d) and Subsections 127(9), 127(18)–(20))

Under paragraph 37(1)(d) and subsections 127(9), 127(18), and 127(19) of the ITA and the CRA Assistance and Contract Payments Policy, SR&ED tax incentives apply only to a claimant's net costs of performing SR&ED in Canada. Consequently, both the Section 37 deductible SR&ED expenditure pool (Lines 429 and 431) and Total Qualified SR&ED Expenditures for ITC purposes (Lines 513, 514, 516, and 518) must be reduced by any government assistance, non-government assistance, or (for ITC purposes) contract payments in respect of SR&ED that the claimant has received, is entitled to receive, or can reasonably be expected to receive on or before the filing-due date of its income tax return for the taxation year.

Under subsection 127(9), government assistance means assistance from a government, municipality, or other public authority—whether as a grant, subsidy, forgivable loan, deduction from tax (including all provincial and territorial R&D tax credits), investment allowance, or any other form of assistance—other than the federal SR&ED ITC itself, and extends to indirect government funding received through non-profit organizations under paragraph 12(1)(x). Non-government assistance means any inducement, reimbursement, contribution, or allowance from a non-governmental entity that would be included in income under paragraph 12(1)(x). Under subsection 127(18), assistance and contract payments reduce qualified SR&ED expenditures on a project-by-project basis down to nil, and under subsection 127(19) any unapplied excess reduces the qualified expenditures of non-arm's length persons for SR&ED they performed (non-arm's length parties may allocate assistance using Form T1145 under subsection 127(20)). When previously deducted assistance is subsequently repaid, the repayment increases the Section 37 pool under paragraph 37(1)(c) (Line 445) and qualifies for an ITC in the year of repayment.
5.2 Stacking Mechanics with Major Canadian Innovation Grants (NRC IRAP, SIF, Mitacs, and ISC)
When stacking federal and provincial innovation grants with SR&ED claims, three operational rules govern the net recovery:

First, under the National Research Council Industrial Research Assistance Program (NRC IRAP)—which reimburses 60% to 80% of direct technical labour costs for eligible Canadian SMEs, including renewed clean-tech support under the Budget 2026 IRAP Clean Technology Initiative—the IRAP grant is deducted as government assistance from the Section 37 pool (Line 429) and from Part 4 qualified expenditures (Line 513). Crucially, however, under Part 5 of Form T661, government assistance does not reduce the Salary Base (Line 818) used to compute the 55% Prescribed Proxy Amount (PPA) on Line 820. Thus, a CCPC receiving an $80,000 IRAP grant on $100,000 of direct SR&ED wages still earns the full $55,000 PPA ($100,000 × 55%), leaving $75,000 in net qualified expenditures ($100,000 salary + $55,000 PPA − $80,000 IRAP grant) that generate an additional $26,250 refundable federal ITC at 35%.

Second, under the Strategic Innovation Fund (SIF) and the $5 billion Strategic Response Fund funded in Budget 2025, government contributions are often structured as forgivable or conditionally repayable loans where repayment depends on future revenues or commercialization milestones. Pursuant to federal jurisprudence (CCLC Technologies Inc. v. The Queen, 96 DTC 6527 (FCA) and Radio Engineering Products Limited v. The Queen, 73 DTC 5071 (FC)), any government loan lacking unconditional repayment terms is classified as government assistance in the year received or receivable, reducing qualified SR&ED expenditures immediately and generating ITCs only when repayments are actually made.

Third, under Mitacs (which provides up to $30,000+ in matching funding for industrial-academic internships) and Innovative Solutions Canada (ISC) (which provides $150,000 to $2,000,000 in R&D funding), grants reduce qualified expenditures as government assistance, whereas procurement contracts to perform SR&ED for a Canadian government or public authority constitute "contract payments" under subsection 127(9) that reduce the contractor's qualified expenditures (with a specific statutory exception for prescribed amounts received from the Canadian Commercial Corporation originating from a foreign government).
6. Provincial and Territorial R&D Tax Credit Regimes

Eight Canadian provinces and one territory administer standalone R&D tax credits. Because all provincial and territorial R&D tax credits constitute "government assistance" under subsection 127(9) of the federal ITA, the provincial credit earned in a taxation year reduces both the federal Section 37 deductible pool (Line 429) and federal Total Qualified SR&ED Expenditures (Line 514) for that same year, unless the taxpayer formally renounces a non-refundable provincial credit where permitted by statute.

body.text: 6.2 Detailed Analysis of Provincial Regimes
1. Québec: The Tax Credit for Research, Innovation and Commercialization (CRIC) (Post-March 25, 2025)

Following Québec's 2025–2026 fiscal reform, the Government of Québec consolidated its R&D tax incentives for taxation years beginning after March 25, 2025, into the Tax Credit for Research, Innovation and Commercialization (CRIC), governed by sections 1029.8.21.16.1 to 1029.8.21.16.31 of the Québec Taxation Act. The CRIC abolished and replaced six former Québec credits: the R&D salaries and wages credit, the university/public research centre credit, the private partnership pre-competitive research credit, the research consortium fees and dues credit, the in-house design credit, and the technological adaptation services credit.

Unlike the former Québec system where rates varied by company asset size, the CRIC provides a size-neutral, 100% refundable two-tier rate structure to startups and multinational corporations alike (except corporations claiming as members of a partnership, for which the 30% enhanced rate does not apply). Specifically, a corporation earns a 30% refundable credit on the first $1,000,000 of qualified expenditures above its applicable exclusion threshold, and a 20% refundable credit on all qualified expenditures exceeding that $1,000,000 tier. The annual exclusion threshold is equal to the greater of $50,000 (adjusted for short taxation years) or the sum of the Québec Basic Personal Amount ($18,571 in 2025) for each employee, prorated by the time spent by each employee on eligible R&D or pre-commercialization activities.

While Québec's R&D definition is harmonized with the federal definition and the CRA performs the scientific review of R&D work, the CRIC also covers eligible pre-commercialization activities undertaken in conjunction with Québec R&D—specifically (a) tests, technological validations, and studies carried out to meet regulatory requirements for obtaining an initial approval or certification to commercialize an innovation (including quality control activities directly related to implementing a quality control system required for initial certification), and (b) product design (form, aesthetics, improved functionality, and choice of materials). Qualified CRIC expenditures include 100% of salaries and wages, 50% of Québec subcontractor payments, 50% of payments to eligible public research centres, research consortia, or university entities, and 100% of capital property acquisition costs (excluding land, buildings, or rights to use land or buildings), claimed on Form RD-1029.8.CR-T (RD-1029.8.CR). Additionally, for taxation years beginning after December 31, 2025, Québec refocused its Tax Credit for Development of E-Business (TCEB / CDAEIA) (30% total rate: 22% refundable and 8% non-refundable in 2026; 21% refundable and 9% non-refundable in 2027) on e-businesses that meaningfully integrate artificial intelligence (AI) functionalities, including data processing and hosting while excluding maintenance or scaling activities.
2. Ontario: Three-Pillar Corporate R&D Tax Credit System

Ontario corporations can claim three provincial R&D tax credits under the Taxation Act, 2007 (Ontario), all administered by the CRA. First, the Ontario Innovation Tax Credit (OITC) (Section 96 / Sections 38 to 45) is an 8% fully refundable tax credit for qualifying corporations on up to $3,000,000 of eligible Ontario SR&ED expenditures, which phases out when prior-year taxable paid-up capital is between $25,000,000 and $50,000,000 or prior-year taxable income is between $500,000 and $800,000. Second, the Ontario Business-Research Institute Tax Credit (OBRITC) (Section 97, claimed on Schedule T2SCH568 with a separate Schedule T2SCH569 for each contract) is a 20% fully refundable tax credit on qualified expenditures incurred in Ontario under an eligible contract with an Eligible Research Institute (ERI) (Ontario universities, colleges of applied arts and technology, hospital research institutes, Ontario Centres of Excellence, and Networks of Centres of Excellence), up to an annual cap of $20,000,000 per associated group (maximum $4,000,000 refundable credit). Third, the Ontario Research and Development Tax Credit (ORDTC) (Sections 38 to 45, claimed on Schedule T2SCH508) is a 3.5% non-refundable credit (with a 3-year carryback and 20-year carryforward) on eligible Ontario SR&ED expenditures reduced by any OITC and OBRITC claimed.
3. Western, Prairie, and Atlantic Provinces and Yukon

In Western Canada, British Columbia offers a 10% refundable SR&ED tax credit for CCPCs and ECPCs up to a $6,000,000 expenditure limit (maximum $600,000 refund, phased out for prior-year taxable capital between $15,000,000 and $75,000,000) and a 10% non-refundable credit (3-year carryback, 10-year carryforward) above the limit or for other corporations, claimed on Form T666 within 18 months of the tax year-end. Alberta provides the refundable Innovation Employment Grant (IEG) (Sections 26.95 to 26.99 of the Alberta Corporate Tax Act, claimed on AT1 Schedule 29 and Form AT4970 within 15 months after the filing due date) on up to $4,000,000 in annual Alberta R&D spending (phased out for taxable capital between $10,000,000 and $50,000,000), paying 8% up to the corporation's base spending level and an enhanced 20% on eligible spending exceeding the base spending level.

In the Prairies, Saskatchewan (Schedule T2SCH403, Sections 63 to 63.4 of The Income Tax Act, 2000 (Saskatchewan)) offers a 10% credit (refundable for CCPCs on up to $2,000,000 of annual qualifying expenditures made on or after December 16, 2024, and non-refundable above that limit or for other corporations, with total credits capped at $1,000,000 per year and an option to renounce non-refundable credits), while Manitoba (Schedule T2SCH380, Section 7.3 of The Income Tax Act (Manitoba)) provides a 15% credit where one-half (7.5%) is refundable and one-half (7.5%) is non-refundable (3-year carryback, 20-year carryforward, or renounced within 6 months of year-end for federal purposes) for in-house R&D, or 15% fully refundable for R&D under contract with a qualifying institute. In Atlantic Canada and the North, Nova Scotia (Schedule T2SCH340, Section 41), New Brunswick (Schedule T2SCH360, Section 59), and Newfoundland and Labrador (Schedule T2SCH301 for corporations / Form T1129 for individuals, Section 42) each provide a 15% fully refundable R&D tax credit, while Yukon (Schedule T2SCH442 for corporations / Form T1232 for individuals, Section 15) provides a 15% fully refundable credit plus an additional 5% refundable credit (20% total) on amounts paid or payable to Yukon University.
7. Governing Bodies, Filing Procedures, Pre-Claim Approval, and Audit Defence
7.1 Governing Authorities and Dual-Track Review Structure

The SR&ED programme is legislated by the Department of Finance Canada and administered across Canada by the Canada Revenue Agency (CRA) (which also conducts the scientific review of R&D work for Revenu Québec under the CRIC). Under subsection 37(3) of the ITA, the Minister of National Revenue may obtain technical advice from the Department of Industry, the National Research Council of Canada, or any other federal research agency. Within the CRA, SR&ED reviews are conducted jointly by a Research and Technology Advisor (RTA) (reporting to a Research and Technology Manager, RTM), who evaluates technical eligibility under subsection 248(1) and prepares the SR&ED Project Eligibility Report, and a Financial Reviewer (FR) (reporting to a Financial Review Manager, FRM), who audits the financial expenditures and calculates the allowable pool and ITC adjustments.
7.2 The Absolute 18-Month Statutory Filing Deadline (Subsections 37(11), 37(11.1), and 37(12))

Under subsection 37(11) and paragraph 127(9)(m) of the ITA and the CRA SR&ED Filing Requirements Policy (updated January 28, 2025), a claimant must file Form T661 together with Schedule T2SCH31 (for corporations) or Form T2038(IND) (for individuals and trusts) containing the prescribed information on or before 12 months after the taxpayer's income tax return filing-due date for the taxation year in which the expenditures were incurred. Because a corporation's T2 filing-due date is 6 months after its taxation year-end, corporations have exactly 18 months after the end of the taxation year to file their SR&ED claim (whereas individuals have 17.5 months after calendar year-end, to mid-June of the second following year).

Under subsections 37(11.1) and 37(12), if the prescribed forms containing the prescribed information are not filed within this 18-month reporting deadline, no amount may be deducted under subsection 37(1), no ITC may be earned, and the expenditures are statutorily deemed not to be expenditures on or in respect of SR&ED. Filing at least 90 days prior to the 18-month deadline gives the CRA sufficient time to perform an initial completeness check and notify the claimant of any deficiencies before the deadline passes.

On May 15, 2026, the CRA published the updated Form T661 (Scientific Research and Experimental Development (SR&ED) Expenditures Claim) and updated Guide T4088-26e to reflect the legislative amendments enacted through Bill C-15.
