body.text: 7.4 The CRA Optional Pre-Claim Approval Process (Launched April 1, 2026)

On April 1, 2026, the CRA launched the optional Pre-Claim Approval Process, enabling eligible businesses to obtain an upfront evaluation of whether their planned R&D projects meet SR&ED technical eligibility requirements before starting work or incurring significant costs. To be eligible to apply, the business must be a CCPC, other Canadian corporation, or partnership, have gross business income of less than $25,000,000, and be in good standing with the CRA; additionally, the project must not have been included in a previous SR&ED claim and must not involve issues currently under litigation. A business can apply for Pre-Claim Approval for up to 3 projects, and each approval is valid for up to 3 years.
The application and evaluation workflow follows four structured steps:

items: Request a Case Number: The business submits a web form to the CRA. Existing SR&ED claimants in good standing are contacted within 2 business days through My Business Account, while all other businesses are contacted within 5 business days by telephone with a Pre-Claim Approval Case Number.

Complete and Submit Form T1322: The applicant completes Form T1322 (Lines 010 to 082)—providing the project title (Line 020), anticipated project start date (Line 022), estimated total SR&ED expenditures (Line 024), technical contact person, Section B technical project descriptions (existing state of knowledge, scientific or technological uncertainty, initial hypothesis, and planned experiments or analyses), and Section C preparer details (Lines 050 to 060)—and uploads the application and supporting business documents in My Business Account.

RTA Evaluation and Meeting: The CRA assigns a Research and Technology Advisor (RTA). For existing SR&ED claimants in good standing, the RTA may request a meeting; for all other businesses, a 2-to-5-hour virtual meeting with the RTA (including screen-sharing slides/documents or a mobile-device facility tour) is mandatory.

Receive Determination Within 8 Weeks: Within 8 weeks of receiving the complete application, the CRA issues a Pre-Claim Approval Evaluation Report confirming whether Pre-Claim Approval is granted and providing the rationale and any recommendations.

body.text: Obtaining Pre-Claim Approval does not replace the annual requirement to file Form T661. When filing Form T661, the claimant ticks Line 212 and enters the Case Number on Line 214. If a pre-approved project is selected for review and has not changed significantly from the approved scope, the CRA reviews only the expenditures and processes the claim within 90 calendar days (compared to the standard 180-calendar-day service standard for refundable claims selected for full review, and 60 calendar days for non-reviewed claims).
7.5 CRA Audit Selection, Dispute Resolution, Objections, and Gross Negligence Penalties
1. Selection for Review, Virtual Audit Process, and Non-Withdrawal Rule

All SR&ED claims undergo risk assessment and may be selected for review based on risk triggers—such as unclear scientific or technological objectives, unclear descriptions of work performed, failure to show systematic investigation, unclear project start or end points, mixing SR&ED with non-SR&ED work, uncorroborated support work, material costs, or contract claims—or random sampling. Once an SR&ED claim is selected for review, it cannot be withdrawn because Form T661 is part of the certified income tax return. Most reviews are conducted virtually via videoconferencing and digital file transfers. Where adjustments or penalties are proposed, the CRA issues a Proposal Package (containing the SR&ED Project Eligibility Report, a proposal letter, and financial calculations), giving the claimant 30 days to submit written representations and supporting evidence.
2. Three-Step Administrative Dispute Resolution and Formal Notice of Objection

Claimants who disagree with review findings can escalate concerns through the CRA's three-step administrative process: (1) discuss concerns directly with the RTA and FR; (2) speak with the reviewers' managers (RTM and/or FRM); and (3) request an Administrative Review upon receiving the proposal package (which checks that the review complied with SR&ED policies, procedures, legislation, and due process). If the claimant still disagrees after the Notice of Assessment or Reassessment is issued, the claimant has the statutory right to file a formal Notice of Objection within 90 days from the date of the Notice of Assessment or Reassessment, and subsequently appeal to the Tax Court of Canada.
3. Gross Negligence Penalties on Overstated SR&ED Claims (Subsection 163(2))

Under subsection 163(2) of the ITA (specifically paragraphs 163(2)(a) and 163(2)(d)) and the CRA Gross Negligence Penalty on Overstated SR&ED Claims Policy (updated January 28, 2025), a penalty applies to every person who, knowingly or under circumstances amounting to gross negligence, makes, participates in, agrees to, or accepts the making of a false statement or omission in an initial or amended return. Under subsection 163(3), the CRA bears the burden of proof on a balance of probabilities to establish that the false statement or omission resulted from more than a simple oversight or misunderstanding of the Act (such as claiming projects known not to involve SR&ED, describing activities that never occurred, claiming personal expenses or fake invoices, or continuing to claim non-qualifying or unsubstantiated amounts after receiving written CRA warnings where the issue is not under objection or appeal).
When the CRA meets this burden of proof, the penalty is equal to the greater of $100 or 50% of the sum of the understated Part I tax payable and the overstated refundable ITC refund claimed:
Penalty = max($100, 50% × [Understated Part I Tax Payable + Overstated Refundable ITC Refund Claimed])

In computing this penalty, the CRA applies strict ordering rules: overstated Section 37 expenditures and overstated ITCs are deemed to be deducted first before valid pool balances or ITCs; under subsection 163(2.1), if a taxpayer is in a net loss position and deducted non-deductible expenses, taxable income is deemed not to be less than zero to compute theoretical Part I tax; and when the gross negligence penalty applies to a refundable ITC refund under paragraph 163(2)(d), the 50% penalty is calculated on the entire overstated refund claimed, even if part of the overstatement stemmed from a simple oversight.
8. Landmark Canadian Jurisprudence and Audit Precedents
Canadian SR&ED administration is governed by a foundational body of jurisprudence from the Tax Court of Canada (TCC), the Federal Court of Appeal (FCA), and the Supreme Court of Canada (SCC).
8.1 Northwest Hydraulic Consultants Limited v. The Queen, 98 DTC 1839 (TCC) and C.W. Agencies Inc. v. The Queen, 2001 FCA 393, 2002 DTC 6740 (FCA)

In Northwest Hydraulic Consultants Limited v. The Queen, 98 DTC 1839 (TCC), Justice Bowman established the landmark five-criteria test—subsequently adopted as the binding national standard by the Federal Court of Appeal in C.W. Agencies Inc. v. The Queen, 2001 FCA 393—to determine whether activities constitute SR&ED under subsection 248(1):

items: Technological Risk or Uncertainty: Was there a technological risk or uncertainty which could not be removed by routine engineering or standard procedures?
Formulation of Hypotheses: Did the person claiming to be doing SR&ED formulate hypotheses specifically aimed at reducing or eliminating that technological uncertainty?
Systematic Investigation (Scientific Method): Did the procedure adopted accord with the total discipline of the scientific method, including the formulation, testing, and modification of hypotheses?
Technological Advancement: Did the process result in a technological advancement?
Detailed Record-Keeping: Was a detailed record of the hypotheses, tests, and results kept as the work progressed?

body.text: 8.2 RIS-Christie Ltd. v. The Queen, 99 DTC 5087 (FCA), Sass Manufacturing Limited v. M.N.R., 88 DTC 1363 (TCC), and Jentel Manufacturing Ltd. v. Canada, 2011 FCA 355 (FCA)

In RIS-Christie Ltd. v. The Queen, 99 DTC 5087 (FCA), Sass Manufacturing Limited v. M.N.R., 88 DTC 1363 (TCC), and Jentel Manufacturing Ltd. v. Canada, 2011 FCA 355 (FCA), the Tax Court and the Federal Court of Appeal reinforced the requirement for structured, systematic experimentation and repeatability. These decisions distinguish systematic investigation under the scientific method—where hypotheses are formulated, tested under controlled conditions, and documented so that results can be verified or reproduced—from routine engineering or trial-and-error shop-floor adjustments.
8.3 116736 Canada Inc. v. Canada, [1998] A.C.I. No. 478 (TCC) and R&D Pro-Innovation Inc. v. The Queen, 2014-1594(IT)G (TCC, 2015)

In R&D Pro-Innovation Inc. (relying on Justice Archambault's analysis in 116736 Canada Inc. v. Canada), Justice Jorré allowed the taxpayer's SR&ED appeal and established two critical evidentiary principles. First, while contemporaneous written records of experiments are highly probative and a taxpayer without them puts itself in a "very precarious position", the existence of contemporaneous documentation is not a mandatory statutory condition for SR&ED recognition under the Act or Regulations; oral testimony can legally establish that eligible SR&ED was performed if found credible by the Court. Second, Justice Jorré cautioned that when a CRA scientific adviser (RTA) testifies before the Tax Court as an expert witness, the adviser must provide an independent opinion grounded in their personal expertise rather than merely applying CRA administrative guidelines and policies.

8.4 Shell Canada Limited v. The Queen (SCC), Data Kinetics Ltd. v. The Queen (TCC), CCLC Technologies Inc. v. The Queen, 96 DTC 6527 (FCA), and Radio Engineering Products Limited v. The Queen, 73 DTC 5071 (FC)

In financial SR&ED disputes, the CRA SR&ED Lease Expenditures Policy cites the Supreme Court of Canada's decision in Shell Canada Limited v. The Queen for the principle that whether an agreement is a lease or a sale must be determined strictly by the legal relationship created by the agreement rather than underlying economic reality (absent a sham or GAAR), and cites Data Kinetics Ltd. v. The Queen for the rule that dedicated bandwidth costs qualify as an equipment lease under the Proxy Method. Similarly, the CRA Assistance and Contract Payments Policy cites CCLC Technologies Inc. v. The Queen, 96 DTC 6527 (FCA) and Radio Engineering Products Limited v. The Queen, 73 DTC 5071 (FC) for the principle that government contributions made to advance public policy—rather than in the exact manner and for the exact commercial reasons of a private business—constitute "government assistance" that reduces qualified SR&ED expenditures even when structured with contingent repayment terms.
9. Comprehensive Financial Modelling and Integrated Federal-Provincial Stacking Case Studies

To demonstrate the exact mathematical interaction of the post-Bill C-15 (S.C. 2026, c. 3) federal rules and provincial tax credit regimes in 2026, this section presents three worked financial case studies.
9.1 Case Study 1: Scaling Ontario CCPC Using the Proxy Method with a Specified Employee, Restored Capital Equipment, and an NRC IRAP Grant (2026 Tax Year)

Consider InnovateAI Corp., an Ontario-resident Qualifying CCPC with a calendar taxation year from January 1, 2026, to December 31, 2026, electing the Proxy Method on Line 160 of Form T661. Its prior-year (2025) taxable capital employed in Canada is $12,000,000 (below the $15,000,000 federal phase-out floor and the $25,000,000 Ontario OITC phase-out floor) and its prior-year taxable income is $300,000 (below the $500,000 federal Qualifying Income Limit and Ontario OITC threshold), giving it the full $6,000,000 federal Expenditure Limit and the full $3,000,000 Ontario OITC limit.

During 2026, InnovateAI Corp. incurs the following SR&ED expenditures in Ontario: (1) Line 300 (Non-Specified Employee Salaries): 10 full-time R&D engineers (100% directly engaged in SR&ED) paid $120,000 each = $1,200,000; (2) Line 305 (Specified Employee Salary): Dr. Sarah Chen (CTO and 25% shareholder), paid a base salary of $260,000 plus a $40,000 bonus, spending 90% (ASA) of her time directly engaged in SR&ED throughout all 365 days of 2026; (3) Line 320 (Materials Consumed): $100,000; (4) Line 340 (Arm's Length SR&ED Contract): $200,000 paid to a taxable supplier; and (5) Line 390 / Line 535 (Restored SR&ED Capital Expenditure): $400,000 for brand-new GPU compute clusters and testing apparatus acquired after December 15, 2024, and used 95% (ASA) of operating time in SR&ED. InnovateAI Corp. receives a $300,000 NRC IRAP grant for its 2026 R&D salaries and renounces its non-refundable 3.5% Ontario ORDTC so that only the refundable 8% Ontario OITC reduces its federal claim.

items: Specified Employee Allowable Salary (Line 305) vs. Proxy Salary Base (Line 816): Dr. Chen's $40,000 bonus is excluded. Because she spent 90% (ASA) of her time directly engaged in SR&ED, 100% of her $260,000 base salary is eligible before the 5 × YMPE cap. For 2026, the YMPE is $74,600, so the 5 × YMPE cap is $373,000 ($74,600 × 5); since $260,000 is below $373,000, Line 305 = $260,000. However, for the Proxy Salary Base on Line 816 (Part 5 Table 7), her inclusion is the lesser of Column 4 ($260,000 × 75% maximum time cap = $195,000) or Column 5 (2.5 × $74,600 YMPE = $186,500), yielding Line 816 = $186,500.

Salary Base (Line 818) and 55% Prescribed Proxy Amount (Line 820 / Line 502): Because the $300,000 NRC IRAP grant does not reduce the Part 5 Salary Base, Line 818 = $1,386,500 ($1,200,000 Line 814 + $186,500 Line 816), and Line 820 / Line 502 (55% PPA) = $762,575.00 (55% of $1,386,500).

Gross Qualified Expenditures and Assistance Reductions: Gross current and PPA qualified expenditures equal $2,482,575.00 ($1,200,000 Line 300 + $260,000 Line 305 + $100,000 Line 320 + $160,000 representing 80% of the $200,000 Line 340 contract + $762,575 PPA), plus $400,000.00 of capital expenditures (Line 535), for $2,882,575.00 total before assistance. Deducting the $300,000 NRC IRAP grant leaves $2,182,575.00 in current qualified expenditures and $400,000.00 in capital qualified expenditures ($2,582,575.00 total), generating an 8% refundable Ontario OITC of $206,606.00 ($174,606.00 on current and $32,000.00 on capital).

Net Federal Qualified Expenditures and 35% Enhanced ITC: Subtracting the $206,606.00 OITC leaves $2,007,969.00 in net federal current/PPA qualified expenditures and $368,000.00 in net federal capital qualified expenditures ($2,375,969.00 total on Line 570). At the 35% enhanced rate, the current/PPA stream generates $702,789.15 (100% cash refundable), and the capital stream generates $128,800.00 (of which 40% = $51,520.00 is cash refundable and 60% = $77,280.00 is a non-refundable ITC).

body.text: 9.2 Case Study 2: Québec Corporation Claiming the New CRIC and Federal SR&ED (Taxation Year Beginning After March 25, 2025)

Consider Montréal Quantum Inc., a Québec-based CCPC with a taxation year from April 1, 2025, to March 31, 2026, subject to both the new Québec CRIC (for taxation years beginning after March 25, 2025) and the Bill C-15 federal SR&ED rules (for taxation years beginning after December 15, 2024). During the year, it incurs $1,200,000 in Québec R&D salaries for 10 full-time R&D employees (non-specified employees, 100% directly engaged in SR&ED), $200,000 for a Québec subcontractor contract, and $300,000 to acquire brand-new R&D laboratory equipment in Québec used 100% (ASA) in SR&ED.

items: Québec CRIC Exclusion Threshold and Refundable Credit (Form RD-1029.8.CR-T): With 10 full-time R&D employees and a 2025 Québec Basic Personal Amount of $18,571 per employee, the employee-based threshold is $185,710 (10 × $18,571); since $185,710 exceeds the $50,000 floor, the Exclusion Threshold = $185,710. Gross CRIC qualified expenditures equal $1,600,000 ($1,200,000 salaries at 100% + $100,000 representing 50% of the $200,000 Québec subcontract + $300,000 capital property at 100%). Subtracting the $185,710 exclusion threshold leaves $1,414,290 in net eligible CRIC expenditures. The CRIC pays 30% on the first $1,000,000 ($300,000.00) and 20% on the remaining $414,290 ($82,858.00), yielding a Total Refundable Québec CRIC of $382,858.00 (of which ($1,300,000 ÷ $1,600,000) × $382,858 = $311,072.13 relates to current expenditures and ($300,000 ÷ $1,600,000) × $382,858 = $71,785.87 relates to capital equipment).

Federal SR&ED Calculation After CRIC Government Assistance: Under the federal Proxy Method, gross federal current and PPA qualified expenditures equal $2,020,000.00 ($1,200,000 Line 300 salaries + $660,000 PPA at 55% of $1,200,000 + $160,000 representing 80% of the $200,000 Line 340 contract), plus $300,000.00 in Line 535 capital expenditures ($2,320,000.00 total). Deducting the $382,858.00 Québec CRIC as government assistance on Line 514 leaves $1,708,927.87 in net federal current/PPA qualified expenditures ($2,020,000 − $311,072.13) and $228,214.13 in net federal capital qualified expenditures ($300,000 − $71,785.87), or $1,937,142.00 total net federal qualified expenditures.

Combined Federal and Québec Recovery: At the 35% enhanced rate, the federal current/PPA stream yields $598,124.75 (100% cash refundable) and the capital stream yields $79,874.95 (of which 40% = $31,949.98 is cash refundable and 60% = $47,924.97 is non-refundable). Together with the $382,858.00 refundable CRIC, Montréal Quantum Inc. receives $1,012,932.73 in total cash refunds (plus $47,924.97 in non-refundable federal ITCs, for $1,060,857.70 in total tax credits on $1,700,000 of cash R&D outlay).

body.text: 9.3 Case Study 3: Eligible Canadian Public Corporation (ECPC) Subject to the Gross Revenue Phase-Out Formula and Shared-Use Equipment (2026 Tax Year)

Consider BioMed Diagnostics Ltd., a TSX-listed Eligible Canadian Public Corporation (ECPC) resident in Canada and not controlled by non-residents, with a calendar taxation year ending December 31, 2026. BioMed's consolidated gross revenues over the three preceding fiscal years (2023, 2024, and 2025) averaged $40,000,000. In 2026, BioMed incurs $5,000,000 in net federal qualified current SR&ED expenditures (including the 55% PPA). Additionally, on January 2, 2025, BioMed acquired and placed into service a brand-new $1,000,000 DNA sequencing machine (not PDP or GPOEF) that was actually used 81% of its operating time (primarily, >50%) for SR&ED in Canada during the First Period running from January 2, 2025, to December 31, 2026 (the first taxation year ending at least 12 months after acquisition), qualifying as First-Term Shared-Use Equipment (SUE) in 2026.

items: ECPC Phased-Out Expenditure Limit (Subsection 127(10.6)): Because BioMed's three-year average gross revenue ($40,000,000) exceeds $15,000,000 by $25,000,000, its $6,000,000 Expenditure Limit is reduced on a straight-line basis across the $60,000,000 phase-out band ($15,000,000 to $75,000,000): ECPC Expenditure Limit = $6,000,000 × (($60,000,000 − $25,000,000) ÷ $60,000,000) = $3,500,000.00

First-Term SUE Inclusion (Line 504): Under subsection 127(9), 1/4 (25%) of the capital cost of the $1,000,000 machine ($250,000.00) is included in qualified expenditures on Line 504 in 2026 (while the $1,000,000 cost is depreciated via regular CCA on Schedule T2SCH8), bringing total qualified expenditures to $5,250,000.00.

Federal ITC and Refundability Calculation: Allocating the $3,500,000.00 Expenditure Limit to current/PPA expenditures yields $1,225,000.00 ($3,500,000 × 35%), which is 100% cash refundable to an ECPC under subsection 127.1(2.01). The remaining $1,750,000.00 of qualified expenditures above the limit ($1,500,000 current + $250,000 SUE) earns the 15% basic rate, generating $262,500.00 in non-refundable federal ITCs (available for 3-year carryback or 20-year carryforward), for a total federal SR&ED benefit of $1,487,500.00.

body.text: 10. Audit Readiness Checklist and Contemporaneous Documentation Protocol
To ensure full statutory compliance and audit readiness under the modernized 2026 Canadian SR&ED framework, claimants should execute the following six-point operational protocol:

items: Contemporaneous Technical Evidence Mapped to the "Why" and "How" Requirements: Capture dated hypotheses, experimental test logs, code commits, photographs, and analytical conclusions as the work progresses rather than reconstructing narratives after year-end, and ensure every project on Form T661 Part 2 includes its mandatory 5-digit CRDC research code on Line 207 and concise responses on Lines 242, 244, and 246.

Upfront Pre-Claim Approval (Form T1322): For corporations or partnerships with gross business income under $25,000,000 launching new R&D projects, request a Pre-Claim Approval Case Number and submit Form T1322 via My Business Account to secure an 8-week upfront technical eligibility determination (valid for up to 3 projects over 3 years) and expedited 90-day expenditure-only reviews upon filing Form T661 (reported on Lines 212 and 214).

Time-Tracking and Specified Employee Payroll Controls: Maintain contemporaneous employee time records allocating hours to specific SR&ED projects, pay all accrued wages within 180 days of year-end (subsection 78(4)), exclude bonuses and profit-based remuneration for specified employees, file Form T1174 with directors' resolutions for specified employees working across associated corporations, and apply the 5 × YMPE ($373,000 in 2026) and 2.5 × YMPE ($186,500 in 2026) / 75% proxy caps.

Capital Property, Shared-Use Equipment, and Equipment Lease Logs: For depreciable property and equipment leases acquired after December 15, 2024, maintain operating-time logbooks tracking SR&ED machine hours against total operating hours to substantiate the 90% ASA intent test for Line 390 capital assets (reporting the top 10 assets on Lines 262 and 263), the >50% actual operating-time test across the 12-month First Period and 24-month Second Period for brand-new Shared-Use Equipment on Line 504 (reporting the top 20 SUE assets in Part 6C Box 792), and the 90% ASA or >50% primarily rules for leased equipment, while excluding used equipment from Line 535 ITC calculations.

CCPC Gross Revenue vs. Taxable Capital Phase-Out Election: For scaling CCPCs whose prior-year associated taxable capital employed in Canada exceeds $15,000,000, compare the taxable capital phase-out (subsection 127(10.2)) against the three-year average gross revenue phase-out election (subsection 127(10.6)) each taxation year to maximize access to the $6,000,000 enhanced 35% Expenditure Limit.

Subcontractor Contracts, Unpaid Amounts, and Part 9 Preparer Disclosures: Maintain signed contracts and statements of work for arm's length Canadian taxable suppliers (Line 340), execute Form T1146 for non-arm's length expenditure transfers (Lines 510 and 540), attach Form T1263 for third-party payments (Line 370), identify any non-salary expenditures unpaid at the 180-day mark on Line 520 within the 18-month reporting deadline, and accurately complete Part 9 Claim Preparer Information (Lines 935 to 975) to prevent the $1,000 penalty under subsection 162(5.1).
